title: Classical Communication Protocol based on Joint Classical-Quantum Coding
authors: Kristian Skafte Jensen, René Bødker Christensen, Čedomir Stefanović, Petar Popovski
abstract: We introduce a robust quantum communication protocol that integrates classical error-control coding, entanglement distribution, and superdense coding. Classical error-correcting codes are used to mitigate dark counts and photon losses by determining the positions of qubit transmissions and protecting the data embedded through superdense coding. We derive conditions on the employed codes that guarantee successful error correction under a bounded error-frequency model. Moreover, upper bounds are derived on the performance of conventional superdense coding protected by classical error correction. It is shown that, under the same constraints on error frequency, suitable code configurations of the proposed protocol can exceed those upper bounds both in terms of data rate and energy efficiency. Finally, we develop a physical error model based on fiber attenuation, detector efficiency, dark counts, and time-slot duration, and use it to evaluate the effective performance of different configurations of error-correcting codes. The proposed approach is primarily suited for short-distance quantum links, as in Quantum Local Area Network (QLAN) where it can provide high communication throughput while integrating entanglement distribution directly into the communication process.
summary: This paper proposes a novel quantum communication protocol that merges classical error-correcting codes with superdense coding to enhance robustness against photon loss and dark counts. By analyzing the system's performance over short-distance quantum links, the authors demonstrate that their joint coding approach surpasses the theoretical limits of conventional error-corrected superdense coding. This makes it highly relevant for developing practical Quantum Local Area Networks (QLANs).
main_problem: To develop a robust quantum communication protocol that integrates classical error-control coding, entanglement distribution, and superdense coding to combat channel impairments like dark counts and photon losses.
main_result: The proposed joint classical-quantum coding protocol can exceed the upper bounds derived for conventional error-corrected superdense coding in terms of both data rate and energy efficiency.
method: The protocol uses classical error-correcting codes to protect data encoded via superdense coding across quantum channels, deriving conditions for successful error correction under a bounded error-frequency model.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as short-distance quantum links, specifically suited for Quantum Local Area Networks (QLAN), operating under physical error sources like fiber attenuation, detector efficiency, and dark counts.
key_observables: Data rate (R), Energy efficiency (E), and the effective rate ($R_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: Fiber length (L), detector efficiency ($E_{det}$), dark count rate ($	au$), and the structure of the employed error-correcting codes (e.g., Hamming, BCH).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes perfect EPR pair generation and is primarily limited to short-distance quantum links due to attenuation being the dominant impairment.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the encoding scheme, compare the proposed protocol's performance against superdense coding upper bounds, and show sensitivity analyses (Tornado diagrams, heat maps) regarding physical channel parameters.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the joint protocol, derives performance bounds and conditions on codes, develops a physical error model, and finally compares the resulting effective rate against established superdense coding limits.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the practical limitations of quantum communication by integrating classical coding theory to enhance performance metrics like rate and efficiency in near-term quantum network architectures.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Illustrative example of the idea behind the proposed encoding scheme. The string of information bits is fed into the signal splitter which encodes chunks of length k given some [n, k, d] code. The ’1’s from the codeword are transmitted using qubits, the pairs of which are entangled and superdense encoding, representing additional bits from the input stream.

Fig. 2. Proposed protocol to manage bit flip errors caused by dark counts and photon losses using classical error-correcting codes. The transmitting user U1 communicates bits to the receiving user U2, by sending the qubits of an EPR pair through a quantum channel, in a slotted setting. These bits are determined by codewords generated as in Fig. 1. The quantum transmission occurs each time a ‘1’ appears in the codeword. When the second qubit of the pair has to be transmitted, two extra information bits are superdense encoded in the EPR pair to enhance the data throughput.

Fig. 3. Rate (black) and lower bound on N (red) for the protocol capable of correcting dark counts using the [2m −1, 2m −m−1, 3] Hamming code, under the assumption that no more than a single dark count occurs for every N time slots.

Fig. 4. Illustrative example of the idea behind the encoding scheme utilizing two error-correcting codes. Information is divided into two separate strings, B and SD; the former is fed into the encoder using Cout, and the latter is fed into the encoder using Cin. The codeword produced by Cin is then used as bits to encode via superdense coding as in Fig. 1.

Fig. 5. Rate and lower bound on N for the protocol capable of correcting both dark counts and photon losses. Here, “Hamming” refers to the scheme using the [2m−1, 2m−m−1, 3] Hamming code as Cout and the [2m, 2m− m −1, 4] extended Hamming code as Cin, while “Hadamard” refers to the scheme using the [2k, k, 2k−1] Hadamard code as Cout and the code defined in Eq.
